Some authors consider the system “plant – herbivore – coprophagous insects” a complex system, since management must meet the requirements of the plants (e.g., fertilization, regrowth), and consumption of fresh mass by the animals $( e . g . ,$ grazing time, capacity) without adversely affecting the community of dung beetles on site (Lobo et al., 2006; Verdú et al., 2007). In Europe, for example, moderate grazing has been considered a positive factor for conservation of dung beetle communities (Lobo et al., 2006; Numa et al., 2009; Buse et al., 2015; Tonelli et al., 2018, 2019). In addition, the abandonment of cattle grazing with the suspension of grazing for an extended period and/or irregular spatial distribution for grazing favor the decline in dung beetle diversity (Lobo, 2001; Carpaneto et al., 2007). In the Neotropical region, there are very few studies that have explored the effect of cattle grazing removal on dung beetle communities in introduced pastures. Alvarado et al. (2019) evaluated how livestock intensification affects dung beetle assemblage structure in cattle ranches. Correa et al. (2019) have evaluated the effect of cattle grazing removal on dung beetle communities in natural grasslands (>20 years of abandonment). This type of studies could help cattle farmers in decision-making for a rotational pasture management aiming at, besides forage production, dung beetle biodiversity conservation.

To evaluate the effect of cattle grazing removal, we compared pastures with different cattle grazing removal times: control (constant presence of cattle, $n = 4 )$ , one $( n = 4 )$ , three $( n = 4 )$ and five months without cattle grazing $( n = 4 )$ . The pastures selected were separated by a minimum distance of 300 m. The distance among pasture sites (300 m) was used to ensure independence of the samples (see da Silva and Hernandez, ´ 2015). Therefore, each pasture site were considered a replicate $(n = 4 sites )$ for each pasture treatment. In each pasture site we installed one linear transect (100 m) located approximately 50 m from the pasture edge for the allocation of the traps. In the transect we demarcated three points separated by 50 m (Fig. 1). At each point we installed a set of two traps separated from each other by 3 m (see Louzada and Carvalho e Silva, 2009). The traps of each set were baited separately with about 40 g of carrion (rotting bovine stomach) and fresh cattle dung. We used different baits in order to ensure an accurate representation of the local dung beetle functional and trophic groups (see Correa et al., 2016a) and in this way we could also evaluate the trophic preferences of each species (dung versus carrion).

Dung beetles were separated and identified at genus level (Vaz-de-- Mello et al., 2011) and then sent to the Universidade Federal de Mato Grosso – UFMT (Cuiaba, ´ Mato Grosso, Brazil) where they were identified at species level by Fernando Z. Vaz-de-Mello. Voucher specimens are deposited in the Entomology Section of the Zoological Collection (CEMT) at the UFMT. To record the biomass of species, all individuals collected were dried $( 4 0 \pm 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ until we got a constant weight and weighed on a 0.0001 g precision scale.

Data were first checked for normality using the Shapiro–Wilk test (Shapiro and Wilk, 1965) and for homoscedasticity using Bartellet’s test. We used Generalized Linear Models (GLMs) to test for differences in species richness, number of individuals and biomass (response variables) of dung beetles among pasture treatments with different cattle removal times (explanatory variables). We used Poisson errors corrected for overdispersion (quasi-Poisson) for dung beetle species richness; negative binomial errors for number of individuals; and Gaussian errors for biomass. All GLMs were submitted to residual analysis to evaluate

To verify differences in species composition among pasture treatments, we used Permutational Multivariate Anova (PERMANOVA) (Anderson, 2001). To test heterogeneity of multivariate dispersions between different pasture treatments, we used permutational multi-variate analysis of dispersion (PERMDISP) (Anderson, 2001). We used a Non-Metric Multidimensional Scaling analysis (NMDS) based on Bray-Curtis dissimilarity matrix with standardized and square-root transformed abundance species data to graphically represent the changes in dung beetle community composition among pasture treatments with different cattle removal times (Anderson and Willis, 2003). PERMANOVA, PERMDISP and NMDS analyses were implemented in the Primer v.6 software with PERMANOVA+ (Clarke and Gorley, 2006).

We calculated community-weighted means of trait values (CWMs) and three functional diversity indexes that measure different aspects of functional diversity, using the R package FD in R software (R Development Core Team, 2020): 1) Functional dispersion (FDis) is estimated as the mean distance of all species to the abundance-weighted centroid of the community in the trait space (Laliberté and Legendre, 2010); 2) Functional evenness (FEve) summarizes how species abundances are distributed along the occupied functional space; and 3) Functional richness (FRic) represents the range of traits in a community quantified by the volume of functional trait space occupied (Villéger et al., 2008).

Ontherus appendiculatus (Mannerheim, 1829) and Trichillum externepunctatum Preudhomme de Borre, 1880 were the most abundant species in our study, representing 39 and 18% respectively, of all individuals sampled (Fig. 2). Species richness $\left( \mathrm{F}_{3,12} = 0.62, p = 0.61; \mathrm{Fig. 3A} \right)$ number of individuals $\chi^{2}{3,12}=2.14,p=0.54; Fig. 3 B), bion mass (F{3,12}=$ $2.17, p = 0.14; Fig. 3 C ),$ Shannon $\left( \mathrm{F}_{3,12} = 0.32, p = 0.80; \mathrm{Fig.~3D} \right)$ and Simpson diversity index $\left( \mathrm{F}_{3,12} = 0.08, p = 0.96; \mathrm{Fig.~3E} \right)$ did not statistically differ among pasture treatments and control.
Community composition did not differ among pasture treatments and control (Pseudo- $F = 1.33, p = 0.15) ( Fig. S1 )$ . In addition, pasture
treatments showed no differences in the multivariate dispersion of points (PERMDISP, F = 2.42, p = 0.36).
